edges-counted-per-face.text: The edges of a solid are counted by adding up the sides of every face (12 pentagons and 20 hexagons give 12 × 5 + 20 × 6 = 180), but each edge belongs to two faces, so every edge is counted twice: halve it to get 90.

region-wrong-coefficient.text: Finding where 24p + 12d = 120 meets the axes by dividing 120 by the wrong price, or by the same number for both axes (p = 5 and d = 5): each axis intercept uses its own price, so p = 120 ÷ 24 = 5 and d = 120 ÷ 12 = 10.

substitute-no-brackets.text: Substituting an expression for a letter without brackets, so a minus or a multiplier only reaches its first term: 2(x − 3) written as 2x − 3.

eliminate-sign-flip.text: Subtracting one equation from the other but forgetting to subtract every term: the sign of the second term in the subtracted equation is left unchanged.

setup-mixed-units.text: Putting quantities in different units into one rule, such as cents for the daily charge and dollars for the rate, so the two plans cannot be compared.

completing-square-corner.text: The number after the bracket is copied from the original (x² + 8x + 3 = (x + 4)² + 3); the bracket (x + 4)² already holds a corner of 16, so that has to be taken away: 3 − 16 = −13.

zero-product-nonzero.text: Each bracket is set equal to the number on the right ((x + 5)(x − 3) = 20, so x + 5 = 20 or x − 3 = 20); a product can only be split like that when it equals 0, so everything is moved to one side first.

decay-means-linear.text: A table that falls every year is called a straight line without testing the drops (30000, 24000, 19200, 15360 'goes down by about 6000, so it's a line'); a line drops the same dollars each time, and these drops (6000, 4800, 3840) aren't equal. Equal ratios (0.8 each year) mean an exponential, and a table that disagrees with a wrong model isn't wrong.

growth-factor-is-rate.text: A growth of 5% a year is written as the factor 0.05 (A = 1000 × 0.05ⁿ); the factor keeps the whole balance and adds 5% of it, so it is 1.05. A factor below 1 shrinks the balance.

one-time-comparison.text: One comparison at a single time (B is bigger at 10 years) is taken to settle which plan is better at every time; the leader can change where the graphs cross, so check a time on each side.

circle-centre-sign.text: The centre of (x − 3)² + (y + 1)² = 16 is read by copying the signs from the brackets, (−3, 1); the centre is where each bracket is zero, (3, −1).

agree-means-accurate.text: Readings that agree with each other are taken to be right (six tape readings within 0.02 m, so the tape is accurate); they can all be wrong the same way, which only a check against a trusted value shows.

all-human-error.text: Any error is put down to 'human error' and fixed by being more careful, so the instrument (a scale that shows 3 g with nothing on it) and the method are never examined; the source decides the fix.

result-error-same-as-input.text: A calculated result is taken to be out by the same amount as the measurements it comes from (lengths out by 0.05 m, so the area is out by 0.05 m²); the errors of both lengths combine, and the area of a 4 m by 3 m room can be out by about 0.35 m².

build-up-no-growth.text: The error of a long job done in many small steps is taken to be one step's error (a 30 m fence laid out with a 1 m ruler, each placement out by 1 cm, so the fence is out by 1 cm); the errors add, up to 30 cm in the worst case.

scale-wrong-direction.text: Going from a plan to the real thing by dividing by the scale (a 5 cm line at 1 : 50 as 5 ÷ 50 = 0.1 cm) or from the real thing to the plan by multiplying; the plan is smaller, so plan to real multiplies and real to plan divides.

plan-units-unconverted.text: A length read from a plan is multiplied by the scale and the answer keeps the plan's unit with a bigger unit's name (8.4 cm × 50 = 420, so the wall is '420 m'); 420 cm is 4.2 m.

pattern-must-continue.text: A pattern that holds for the first few cases (regions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, or forty primes in a row) is taken to hold for every case and to be proved; a pattern only describes the cases checked, and the next case can break it (6 points make 31 regions, not 32).

cone-as-cylinder.text: Finds the volume of a cone as if it were the whole cylinder with the same base and height (3.14 × 2² × 1.5), instead of one third of it.

join-faces-counted.text: Adds the faces that are joined together when finding the surface area of a composite object (both circles where a cone sits on a cylinder), although they are hidden inside and aren't part of the outside.

hole-added.text: Adds the volume of a hole to the volume of the solid it goes through instead of taking it away, so the object holds more material than the block it was cut from.

proof-assumes-conclusion.text: The statement to be proved is used as the reason for a step ("opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so A = C"); a reason has to be a given fact, a known rule or an earlier line, never the conclusion itself.

depression-from-vertical.text: The angle of depression is measured down from the tower (the vertical) or placed inside the triangle at the top, so the sides swap and tangent is turned upside down; it is measured down from the horizontal, so the same angle sits at the foot of the line of sight, with the height opposite it.

bearing-from-east.text: The bearing's angle is taken from the east line, so east is next to it (cosine) and north is opposite; a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so north is next to the angle (cosine) and east is opposite it (sine).

diagonal-legs-added.text: The floor diagonal and the height are added to give the longest line in a box (94.3 + 30); they are the two shorter sides of a second right-angled triangle, so the space diagonal needs Pythagoras again: the square root of the sum of their squares.

equal-diagonals-enough.text: A theorem is used the wrong way round: because a rectangle's diagonals are equal, a frame with equal diagonals is taken to be a rectangle; the frame must also be a parallelogram first (an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals and no right angles).

fits-here-fits-everywhere.text: A model that matches one measurement is taken to be true for every time; it was only checked near that point, and further out its assumption (steady doubling with unlimited food and room) fails.

one-case-confirms.text: A conjecture is called proved after one or two cases that agree (a = 1 and a = 2 both land sooner, so it is true for every a); agreeing cases only support it, and one case that disagrees rejects it.

scatter-axes-swapped.text: A student's dot is plotted with the two numbers the wrong way round (arm span 150, height 175 plotted across 175 and up 150); the first variable named goes across and the second goes up, so each dot has to be read in that order.

steepness-is-strength.text: A scatterplot is called weak because its dots rise gently, or strong because they rise steeply; strength is how tightly the dots follow one pattern, whatever the steepness.

negative-means-weak.text: A negative association is taken to be a weak one (or a bad one); direction and strength are separate, and dots tight round a falling line are a strong negative association.

association-is-cause.text: Two things that rise together are taken to mean one causes the other (more ice-cream sales cause more drownings); they may both follow a third thing, such as hot weather, or the link may be chance.

percent-of-grand-total.text: Each count in a two-way table is turned into a percentage of everyone in the table, so groups of different sizes are compared unfairly; to compare groups, each row (or column) is turned into a percentage of its own total.

wrong-way-percentage.text: The percentages are made along the wrong direction of the table, so they answer a different question (the share of the cyclists who play sport instead of the share of the sport players who cycle); the question says which total to divide by.

table-shows-cause.text: A pattern in the percentages of a two-way table is reported as one thing causing the other (students who ride to school play more sport, so riding makes them sporty); a table only shows that the two seem linked in the people asked.

vague-question.text: An investigation question names no two variables, or mixes them up (Do students sleep well? or Does sleep matter?); a good question names both variables, how each is measured and which one is expected to affect the other.

conditional-direction-swapped.text: P(A | B) is found inside the wrong group: the chance of a cloudy morning given rain is divided by the cloudy mornings (30 out of 50) instead of the rainy days (30 out of 40); the given event is the group you look in.

base-rate-ignored.text: A test that is right for 9 in 10 people with the condition is taken to mean 9 in 10 people who test positive have it; the chance given a positive test is found inside the positives, which include people without the condition, so it can be much lower when the condition is rare.

dependent-by-counts.text: Two events are called dependent because the counts differ (18 walkers play sport but 42 non-walkers do); independence compares rates, P(A | B) with P(A), because the groups have different sizes.

sim-differs-so-wrong.text: A simulation result that differs from the calculated chance (0.31 against 0.27) is taken to show the calculation is wrong; a simulation of a few hundred trials wanders, and it settles near the calculated chance as the trials grow.

quartile-halfway-to-extreme.text: The lower quartile is found as the point halfway between the lowest value and the median, as if it were a distance; it is the median of the lower half of the ordered values.

box-width-is-count.text: The width of a box is read as how many values there are; both halves of a boxplot hold about the same number of values, and the width shows how far apart the quartiles are (the spread of the middle half).

compare-centre-only.text: Two data sets are compared by their medians alone and the one with the lower or higher median is called better; the box length, whiskers and outliers say how much the values vary, which matters for something like reliability.

area-sets-the-count.text: The number of sprinklers is taken to depend only on the oval's area (area ÷ the area of one circle); the shape matters and circles leave gaps, so a long thin oval needs more than a square one of the same area.

placement-at-cell-edge.text: A sprinkler is placed at the end of its cell (x = i × w) instead of the middle (x = (i − 0.5) × w); the cell is only covered when the sprinkler sits in the middle, so the far corner of each cell is out of reach.

typed-answer-stale.text: The answer is worked out by hand and typed into a cell, so the sheet holds only a number; when a cell it came from changes, the typed answer stays the same and is silently wrong.

row-before-column.text: A cell's name is written row first (3D, 2C), when it is the column letter then the row number (D3, C2); the headings at the top and side of the sheet show which is which.

same-formula-every-row.text: The same formula text is typed into every row (or the formula is copied as text), so every row keeps working on the first row's cells; a copied formula moves its cell names to its own row, so each row uses its own cells.

fixed-cell-moves.text: A formula that needs one shared cell (such as g) is copied without fixing that cell, so its name moves down with each copy and points at an empty cell, which counts as 0; a $ in front of the column letter and the row number keeps the name where it is.

comma-not-colon.text: A comma is used between the first and last cell (=SUM(B2,B8)), so only those two cells are added; a colon names every cell between them (B2:B8), while a comma only lists the cells it names.

zero-for-missing.text: A 0 is typed for a measurement that was not taken, so the sheet counts a real value of 0 and AVERAGE and MIN come out too low; an empty cell is skipped by AVERAGE, MIN and MAX, so a missing measurement should be left empty.

words-need-quotes.text: The words in an IF answer are written without quote marks (=IF(B2>=10,Tall,Short)), so the sheet takes Tall and Short for names it does not know and shows #NAME?; words in a formula go inside quote marks.

sort-one-column.text: Only one column of a table is selected and sorted, so that column moves while the others stay where they are and every row now mixes numbers from different items; sorting needs the whole table so that whole rows move together.

pie-for-change.text: A pie chart is chosen for numbers that are not parts of one whole, such as a temperature each minute, so the slices look alike and the change over time cannot be seen; a pie shows how one whole is shared and a line chart shows change over time.

fake-heading.text: A line is made bold and bigger by hand so it looks like a heading, but its style is still Body text; the app cannot see it, so it is missing from the headings panel and contents list and a screen reader cannot jump to it.

restyle-by-hand.text: Every heading is changed by hand, one at a time, instead of changing its style once; a new heading added later does not match, and by-hand formatting stays on top of the style.

order-needs-numbers.text: Steps that must happen in order are put in a bulleted list, so the reader cannot tell which comes first or how many there are; a numbered list shows the order.

list-for-table.text: Facts that each have several values (a condition and its height) are put in a bulleted list, so they cannot be compared at a glance; a table with a header row lines up the values in columns.

cram-the-page.text: The margins and spacing are squeezed so everything fits on fewer pages, and the page is hard to read; white space is part of the layout, not wasted paper.

slide-is-a-page.text: A paragraph or a whole report section is copied onto one slide, so the audience reads instead of listening and the slide holds many ideas; a slide carries one.

decoration-picture.text: A picture is added because it looks nice, not because it shows something the words cannot; it takes space and attention and says nothing about the idea.

low-contrast.text: Pale text is put on a pale background, or small text on a slide, because it looks soft on the screen in front of you; from the back of the room it cannot be read.

no-credit-needed-online.text: A picture or text found online is treated as free for anyone to use, without a credit or a look at the licence; someone made it, and the licence says what you may do.

final-final-name.text: A file is named final, final-final or new instead of saying what it is and when; those words stop being true as soon as another version is saved.

copy-is-move.text: Dragging a file is assumed to copy it (or to move it) without looking where it is afterwards; drag can do either, depending on where it is dropped.

only-one-copy.text: Work is kept in one place only, so one failure loses it; a backup is a copy in a different place.

change-everything.text: Several things are changed at once when something goes wrong, so it is not known which change helped.

delete-takes-it-back.text: Deleting a post or message is thought to take it back from everyone; anyone who saw it before it was deleted may have saved, screenshotted or passed it on.

private-means-private.text: A private account or a small group is thought to mean only the chosen people will ever see a post; anyone in the audience can screenshot or forward it to people outside.

joke-is-fine-if-meant.text: A message is judged by what the sender meant, so a joke is fine if it was meant as one; the person reading it sees only the words, without the tone or the face.

friendly-means-trusted.text: Someone online who is friendly, shares the same interests or says they are the same age is taken to be who they say; a friendly profile can be made by anyone, so personal details and secrets wait until a trusted adult has checked.

rush-means-real.text: A countdown, a prize or 'everyone has it' is taken as a reason to act now; pressure to hurry is a sign to slow down, check and ask.

tell-means-trouble.text: Telling a trusted adult is thought to get you in trouble or make things worse, so a problem is kept secret or deleted; telling early, and keeping what happened, is how things get fixed.

top-result-is-best.text: The first search result is clicked and trusted because it is first; it may be an advert, out of date or about another place, and its position is not a check.

pages-just-inform.text: A page is treated as neutral information without asking who made it or why; a page made to sell or persuade may still be right, but it is read knowing what it wants.

looks-mean-trust.text: A polished, exciting page is trusted over a plain one because of how it looks; design, big numbers and confident words are not reasons, and an author, a date and a source are.

many-copies-agree.text: Every page that repeats a claim is counted as more evidence; pages that copied the first are one source, and a check needs places that found it out themselves.

sure-sounding-is-fact.text: A statement is taken as a fact because it sounds sure, or because the reader agrees with it; a fact is something that could be checked, and sales lines and opinions often sound just as sure.

shape-not-numbers.text: A chart or a percentage is read by its shape or size without checking the axis, the whole or how many were counted; true numbers can still give the wrong idea.

picture-is-proof.text: A real picture is taken as proof of what its caption says; the caption, the date or the crop can be wrong even when the picture is real.

ai-checks-itself.text: An AI answer is checked by asking the same AI (or another chatbot) if it is sure; that is the same kind of source again, and a check needs a place that would know.

one-source-is-enough.text: An answer is built on one source, often the one with the most exciting claim, instead of what several trusted sources agree on; the answer then says more than the evidence shows.

nearest-noun.text: A pointing word (it, she, they) is taken to mean the closest noun before it, without checking that the sentence still makes sense with that noun swapped in.

connective-sounds-clever.text: A joining word is chosen because it sounds grown-up or formal (however, therefore), without asking how the two ideas actually connect, so it signals the wrong relationship.

start-with-new.text: A sentence starts with something brand new instead of picking up what the reader already knows, so the thread of the paragraph snaps and the reader has to hold the new idea until the end of the sentence to see what it is about.

never-repeat.text: Repeating a key word is treated as always bad style, so it or they is used even where it could point to two things, and the reader loses track of which one is meant.

general-before-specific.text: A general word (the vehicle, the animal) is used before the specific thing it stands for has been named, so the reader has nothing to link it to and pictures something else.

detail-off-topic.text: A sentence that does not belong to the paragraph's topic sentence is left in (or the first sentence is taken to be the topic sentence by habit), so the paragraph wanders and the reader cannot tell what it is about.

new-idea-in-conclusion.text: A conclusion is used to add a new fact or point that no body paragraph covered, instead of pulling together what the text has already said.

quote-speaks-for-itself.text: A quotation or example is given after a claim and treated as if it proves the claim on its own, with no explanation of how the evidence supports it, so the reader has to do the writer's thinking.

fast-means-right.text: An answer that comes quickly and feels obvious must be right, so it needs no check; a fast first answer is often the wrong one, and a quick check (putting it back into the question) catches it.

chose-it-so-regulated.text: Choosing your own goal means you are steering your learning well; choosing what to learn (self-directed) is different from planning, checking and adjusting how you learn it (self-regulated).

easy-means-learned.text: If studying feels easy and familiar, you have learned it; familiarity from rereading can feel like knowing, and only a check without the notes shows what you can actually do.

one-strategy-for-everything.text: One study or problem-solving strategy works for every kind of stuck; the right strategy depends on what is going wrong (not understanding the task, no plan, an answer that does not fit, or not knowing if you know it).

stage-missing.text: A stage the reader needs is left out (most often the orientation of a recount, so it starts with 'Then...'), because the writer already knows who, where and when and forgets the reader doesn't.

feature-wrong-type.text: A feature that belongs to a different kind of text slips in (an opinion or a story moment in an information report), because the writer is thinking about the topic, not what the text is for.

phase-out-of-order.text: The phases of an explanation sequence are written in the order the writer remembers them, not the order they happen, so a step depends on one the reader hasn't met yet.

purpose-drift.text: A text starts with one purpose and drifts into another (a report on frogs turns into a recount of the class excursion), because the writer follows the topic instead of the purpose.

pattern-half.text: A compare-and-contrast (or cause-and-effect) paragraph gives only one side: it describes one thing in detail and never says how the other is alike or different, so the pattern is announced but not carried out.

main-point-buried.text: The most important point is saved until the end of a report or news item, so a reader in a hurry never reaches it; information texts usually put it first.

wrong-audience.text: The structure and words suit the writer, not the reader (long technical sentences in a text for young children), because the writer doesn't picture who will read it.

hybrid-no-link.text: A story is added to an argument (or a recount to a report) but never linked back to the point, so the reader enjoys the story and misses why it is there.

clause-alone.text: A dependent clause is left standing as a sentence on its own ('Because the water was high.'), because it was written as an answer to a question or as an afterthought and it feels complete to the writer who knows the rest.

speech-not-shifted.text: A report drops the quotation marks but keeps the speaker's own words ('Max said that I am hungry'), because the writer changes the punctuation and forgets that the speaker's pronouns and tense belong to the person speaking, not the one reporting.

wrong-relationship.text: A joining word gives a different relationship from the one the writer means ('although' where 'because' is meant), because the word sounds right as a connector and the writer does not check what it says about how the two ideas relate.

vague-noun.text: A noun group is too thin to picture ('a thing on its face', 'a nice animal'), because the writer can already see what they mean and forgets the reader has only the words.

embedded-misplaced.text: An embedded clause is placed away from the noun it tells about ('a book that sank' for a boat), because the writer attaches it to the nearest word at the end rather than the right noun.

weak-verb.text: A plain verb is propped up with an adverb ('ran very fast') where one precise verb would be sharper, because the first verb that comes to mind is the plain one and the writer adds to it rather than choosing again.

shape-miscount.text: A dependent clause is counted as a second main clause, because any joining word seems to make two equal parts, so a complex sentence is labelled compound.

one-shape.text: A writer uses one sentence shape throughout, or the longest, because long feels more grown-up, so the key point is buried when the reader needs it at a glance.

tense-slip.text: A verb slips into another tense in the middle of a recount because the writer is picturing the scene as it happens, so the time seems to jump.

choppy-pair.text: Two sentences about the same thing are left as two, repeating the noun, because folding feels harder than stopping and starting again.

apostrophe-plural.text: An apostrophe is put on a plain plural because any word ending in s looks as if it needs one, so a word that only means more than one is treated as an owner.

opening-phrase-comma.text: A long phrase at the start of a sentence is left without a comma, because the reader can follow it without a pause and the writer does not hear where the main part starts.

comma-as-pause.text: A comma goes wherever the voice pauses, even between a subject and its verb, so the writer splits a sentence where it should stay whole.

colon-mid-clause.text: A colon goes wherever a list or reason follows, even in the middle of a clause such as after 'because', so the writer splits a clause that is not yet complete.

comma-splice.text: A comma is enough to join two sentences, so the writer sticks two main clauses together with a comma alone.

one-register.text: Writing the same way to everyone, without noticing that a friend and a principal need different words.

synonyms-interchangeable.text: A synonym can be swapped in for any similar word, so the shade or strength of meaning is ignored.

command-to-authority.text: Giving an order to someone in charge, because the writer does not notice that a request is expected.

polite-is-formal.text: Treating a friendly, polite line as formal, because being kind and being official are not told apart.

familiarity-only.text: Choosing words using only how well the reader is known, and leaving out that the reader has authority.

language-judged.text: Judging a person's character from how they speak, when every way of speaking is valid for its group.

insider-language.text: Using a group's acronyms and special words with a newcomer without explaining them, so the newcomer is left out.

opinion-in-report.text: Putting an opinion into a report, so the writing sounds like a view and not a finding.

bare-assertion.text: Treating a claim as proven because it sounds sure or because everybody says so, when nothing backs it up.

any-source-counts.text: Treating any named or reported source as strong evidence, whether or not it knows about the claim.

emotive-in-news.text: Using emotive words in a report that is meant to stay neutral, so the report pushes a feeling.

both-sides-balanced.text: Believing a report is balanced because it names both sides, even when its word choices favour one.

claim-without-backing.text: Making a judgement and giving no detail or source, so a reader has nothing to check.

feature-misnamed.text: Naming a language feature wrongly, so the explanation of its effect does not fit.

device-effect-flipped.text: Giving a device the wrong effect, such as saying understatement makes a problem sound bigger.

effective-without-reason.text: Calling a language choice good or effective without saying for whom or why.

close-new-idea.text: A new idea is put into the close of a talk, where the listener has no time to take it in, because the speaker remembers something at the end instead of fixing the plan.

read-it-out.text: A script is written like an essay and read out, with long sentences and clauses tucked in the middle, because the writer is thinking of a reader who can look back, not a listener who hears it once.

cards-are-script.text: The cue card holds the whole script copied out, so the speaker reads it instead of speaking, because writing more on the card feels safer than trusting the key words.

register-one-size.text: One way of speaking is used for every audience (a joke-filled chat to the principal, or a formal speech to a Year 5 class), because the speaker picks the register they are most comfortable with, not the one the listeners expect.

voice-one-setting.text: A talk is delivered in one steady pace, volume and tone from start to finish, because the speaker aims to get through it, not to use the voice to show what matters.

transcript-has-voice.text: A transcript is judged as if it showed how the talk sounded, when a transcript has the words only; pace, pitch, volume and pauses are not on the page unless someone marked them.

slides-repeat-speech.text: The slides repeat what the speaker says, word for word, so the listeners read ahead and stop listening, because the speaker uses the slide as the script.

feedback-vague.text: Feedback after a rehearsal is general ('it was good', 'speak up') and cannot be acted on, because the listener names a feeling and not what they heard or saw.

enough-stuff-ends-wanting.text: Wants are treated as a supply problem: if enough was made, everyone would have all they want and wanting would stop. In fact meeting one want tends to bring another, so wants do not run out.

needs-wants-blur.text: A thing is called a need because it is expensive, popular or makes the student sad to lack, instead of because they cannot stay safe and well without it.

shortage-vs-scarcity.text: Scarcity is taken to mean something ran out for a day, so ordering more stock would end it. A shortage is short-term and fixed by stock; scarcity is the lasting gap between unlimited wants and limited land, labour and capital.

opportunity-cost-is-price.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is given as the price paid, or as everything not chosen. It is the next best alternative given up, one thing.

parliament-changes-constitution.text: The Constitution is treated as an ordinary law that Parliament can change whenever it votes to. In fact it sits above ordinary laws and limits Parliament, so a change has to be approved by the voters at a referendum.

recall-is-inquiry.text: A question about the topic with one fact for an answer ('When did the Han dynasty start?') is taken to be a good inquiry question because it is about history or geography. An investigable question needs evidence to be gathered and weighed before it can be answered.

topic-word-is-question.text: A big-idea word such as 'scarcity' or 'change' is written down as the question. It names the topic. A question has to ask something about it that evidence can answer.

bigger-question-better.text: A bigger question ('What is democracy?') is thought to make a better investigation. It is too big to answer with the evidence a class can gather; a right-sized question names the case and can be answered from sources it can find.

first-result-is-the-place.text: The first search result, or the first place that comes to mind, is taken as the right place to look. The right place depends on what the question needs: a count, a decision, a record, a view.

interesting-is-relevant.text: A fact that is interesting or true is kept as though it helped answer the question. It is only worth keeping if it bears on the question being asked.

notes-in-order-found.text: Notes are left in the order they were found, or sorted by source. Grouped under the sub-questions they help answer, they show what is missing and what to say first.

old-means-primary.text: A source is sorted as primary because it is old, or secondary because it is recent. The test is whether it was made at the time of the event being investigated: a very old history written long after is secondary, and a recent diary of a recent event is primary.

origin-from-content.text: Who made a source is read off what it shows (a soldier made the clay soldier). What a source shows is its content; who made it, when and where is its origin.

context-is-setting.text: Context is given as the place or period ('ancient China') instead of what was going on when the source was made.

purpose-is-content.text: Purpose is given as what the source shows or says ('it shows the emperor') instead of why it was made and what the maker wanted it to do.

one-question-enough.text: One broad question is taken to be enough for an inquiry. An inquiry needs smaller questions about what, where, who and why to cover the parts of the big one.

continuous-is-renewable.text: A continuous resource such as sunlight is treated as the same as a renewable one because both 'come back'. A renewable resource comes back only if it is used no faster than it renews, so it can be used up. A continuous resource cannot be used up by what people do.
